Validation Against Published Results

Source: vignettes/articles/validation.Rmd
validation.Rmd

Every sequential procedure in SMSD comes from a published source, and most of those sources report what the procedure does: a simulation table, a worked example, or a result that can be computed exactly. This article sets the package beside those reports. It shows where the package reproduces them, where it does not, where it differs on purpose and why, and, at the end, what the procedures do not deliver when the target is wide.

Nothing is simulated when this page is built. The numbers come from one script, data-raw/validation_study.R in the package’s repository, which runs each procedure through the package’s exported functions and saves the results. The page reads that file:

results <- readRDS(file.path("..", "..", "data-raw", "validation_results.rds"))
dim(results)
#> [1] 304  15
names(results)
#>  [1] "family"           "procedure"        "source"           "condition"       
#>  [5] "quantity"         "published"        "published_se"     "published_digits"
#>  [9] "value"            "se"               "replications"     "kind"            
#> [13] "mean_n"           "note"             "z"
c(date = attr(results, "date"), SMSD = attr(results, "package_version"),
  seed = attr(results, "seed"))
#>         date         SMSD         seed 
#> "2026-10-10"      "1.0.0"   "20261010"

The study took 94 minutes on 6 cores (493 minutes of processor time). Each simulated condition was run in 20 parts with their own seeds, so the results do not depend on the number of cores, and the script can be run again to check them (see the last section).

How to Read the Tables

Each table sets a value from a source beside the value the package gives for the same condition.

  • The package’s value comes from the exported functions only. Where a *_sensitivity() function generates the article’s data, that function ran the procedure. Otherwise the pilot function and the check function were called in the loop a study would run: start at the pilot sample size, add one observation, check, and stop the first time the check reports the stopping rule as met.
  • SE is the Monte Carlo standard error of the package’s value.
  • z is the package’s value minus the published value, divided by the standard error of that difference. The standard error combines three things: the Monte Carlo error of the package’s value, the Monte Carlo error of the published value where that value is itself a simulation mean, and the rounding of the published value to the decimals printed. For the Monte Carlo error of a published mean the study uses the standard error that the article prints. Where an article prints none (the mean widths of the 2018 tables and of the squared multiple correlation tables, for example), it uses the standard error that the spread found in this study gives a mean of the article’s 5,000 replications. A value of z between -2 and 2 is what chance alone produces 95 times in 100. With several thousand replications on each side the comparison is sharp: a z of 5 can belong to a difference in the fourth decimal.
  • Replications is the number of simulated studies behind the package’s value. It is empty where the value is not simulated.
  • N is the final sample size: the number of observations at which the procedure stopped.

The reproduction sections below hold 175 comparisons of a simulated value from the package with a published simulation value, a population value, or an exact value, so a few values of z beyond 2 are expected by chance alone even where the package and the source agree exactly. (The cached file has 304 rows in all. The others are worked examples and closed forms, which have no sampling error; rows in which the package departs from its source on purpose, or in which a rule as printed is simulated in place of the package’s; and rows set beside a nominal level or a bound and not beside a published value, most of them in the last section.) Where the reference value is exact, a difference of more than three standard errors can only be chance or a defect, and the study settles which by running that condition a second time, with new seeds and ten times the replications; both runs are shown. A row that does not reproduce is shown as it is.

A Narrow Confidence Interval: Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018)

Tables 2 to 4 of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018, pp. 233–234) report the mean final sample size, the coverage, and the mean width of the interval for the standardized mean difference (95% intervals no wider than 0.2) and for the coefficient of variation (90% and 95% intervals no wider than 0.04). The rows below are the two normal conditions of Table 2 with standardized mean differences of 0.3 and 0.5, and the normal, gamma, and lognormal populations with a coefficient of variation of 0.2 from Tables 3 and 4. For the standardized mean difference the sample size is per group.

Of the 24 comparisons, 24 are within two standard errors and the largest difference is 1.7 standard errors. The package reproduces these tables.

One detail of the comparison needs a note. The article’s tables print a column s(N) described as the standard error of the mean final sample size, and its entries are far too small to be that. For the standardized mean difference of 0.5 the entry is 0.0026, while the standard deviation of the final sample size in this study is 13.0, which gives a mean of 5,000 replications a standard error of 0.18. (The printed entry is close to that standard deviation divided by 5,000.) The standard error of each published mean final sample size in this section is therefore computed from the standard deviation found here and the article’s 5,000 replications. The tables print no standard error for the mean width, so its standard error is computed in the same way.

Correlation Coefficients: Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2019)

The rows are from Table 2 (Pearson, p. 498), Table 8 (Kendall, p. 502), and Table 10 (Spearman, p. 503) of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2019): bivariate normal data and 95% intervals. The Pearson rows were run by seq_aipe_r_sensitivity(); that function studies the Pearson correlation only, so the Kendall and Spearman rows were run through seq_aipe_r_pilot() and seq_aipe_r(). The coverage of a rank correlation is counted against its own population value (0.3333 for Kendall and 0.4826 for Spearman when ρ = 0.5, as the article gives them).

Pearson, rho = 0.1; width 0.2 5,000 372.2 372.2 (0.6) 0.0 0.9396 0.9392 (0.0034) -0.1 0.1992 0.1994 1.9
Pearson, rho = 0.5; width 0.2 10,000 204.0 205.5 (0.5) 1.7 0.9012 0.9119 (0.0028) 2.1 0.1938 0.1959 4.9
Pearson, rho = 0.5; width 0.1 4,000 857.0 856.8 (1.3) -0.1 0.9464 0.9487 (0.0035) 0.5 0.0998 0.0998 -0.3
Kendall, rho = 0.1; width 0.2 5,000 170.9 174.0 (0.2) 13.5 0.9440 0.9420 (0.0033) -0.4 0.1984 0.1981 -9.8
Kendall, rho = 0.5; width 0.2 10,000 133.2 135.9 (0.2) 10.6 0.9318 0.9372 (0.0024) 1.3 0.1972 0.1968 -12.6
Spearman, rho = 0.5; width 0.2 4,000 238.8 239.7 (0.6) 1.1 0.9300 0.9350 (0.0039) 0.9 0.1986 0.1987 1.9

Pearson. The mean final sample sizes are within 1.7 standard errors of the article’s. At ρ = 0.5 and a width of 0.2 the package’s studies run slightly longer, cover slightly more often, and end with slightly wider intervals than the article’s (205.5 against 204.0 pairs, coverage 0.912 against 0.901, mean width 0.1959 against 0.1938, the last a difference of 4.9 standard errors). All three are the effect of a deliberate departure described below: the package does not stop on a variance estimate that is zero or negative. Coverage of about 0.90 at a nominal 0.95 in that row is the article’s own finding, and the package’s too. It is taken up in the last section.

Kendall. The mean final sample sizes and mean widths of these rows do not reproduce. The package’s mean final sample size is 135.9 against the article’s 133.2 at ρ = 0.5 and 174.0 against 170.9 at ρ = 0.1, differences of 11 and 14 standard errors. The final sample size also varies far more from study to study than the article’s standard errors imply: its standard deviation is 20.4 here against 10.7 at ρ = 0.5, about 2 times as large, and 16.0 against 2.6 at ρ = 0.1, about 6 times as large. (With the spread found here in place of the article’s standard errors, the two means are still 8 and 10 standard errors from the article’s.) The differences in the means are small in practical terms, about 2 percent of the sample size and at most 0.0004 in mean width, but they are far outside Monte Carlo error. Coverage does agree with the article’s: 0.937 against 0.932 at ρ = 0.5 and 0.942 against 0.944 at ρ = 0.1, differences of 1.3 and -0.4 standard errors. The package computes the variance estimator of the article’s Equations 27 to 29 (p. 500); its tests compare the code with a transcription of those equations and with the large sample value for bivariate normal data. The cause is therefore most likely a difference between the printed equations and the code behind the article’s table, and it cannot be settled without that code.

Spearman. The row is reproduced within 1.9 standard errors.

Of the 24 mean final sample sizes, 21 are within two standard errors of the article’s and 23 within three (the largest difference is 3.1); of the 24 coverages, 21 are within two and 24 within three (largest 2.2). The one mean that differs by more than three standard errors is within 5.5 observations (1.1 percent) of the article’s. The mean widths agree with the article’s within 0.0004 in every row: of the 24 differences, 23 are within two standard errors and none is more than three (the largest is 2.1). (The tables print no standard error for the mean width; the one used is described under How to Read the Tables.) The low coverages in these tables are the article’s as well as the package’s: 0.667 in the article and 0.668 here for the 5 predictors, population value 0.9 row of the log transformed interval at 90%. The Wald rows are reproduced by a stopping rule that differs in one sign from the article’s Equation 63 as printed; see the departures below.

The one exception is the minimum variance of the mixture block, printed as 0.8486. The article’s own formula gives 8.4788 for the standard deviations that reproduce that block’s three sample sizes, so the printed value appears to be a misprint.

The sequential procedure. For the normal block of Table 1 the article reports the mean final sample size of each group and the mean of the estimated variance over 5,000 studies with a pilot sample of 10 per group (p. 432). seq_budget_sensitivity() ran the same design under both of the package’s procedures. procedure = "first_passage" is the package’s reading of the article’s rule, in which a group is closed for good the first time it meets its criterion; procedure = "reallocate", the default, judges every group on the current data at every step. The first passage option is not a step for step copy of the article’s sequence (the help page of seq_budget_next() lists three differences), so the study also ran that sequence itself, written out step for step from pp. 429–430 of the article in base R with no package code. It is the third block of the table.

The article’s table prints no mean cost. The value in the “Article” column of those rows is the cost its mean final sample sizes imply: the sum over the groups of the cost of an observation (38, 15, and 10) times the mean final sample size. For the estimated variance the table prints a mean absolute deviation (0.0285) and no standard error; z uses a standard error for the article’s mean taken from it by the relation that holds for a normal variable.

The table is reproduced only in part, and the article’s own sequence does not reproduce it either. With the first passage rule the mean final sample sizes of the first two groups agree with the article’s (-1.8 and 0.2 standard errors) and that of the third is higher (41.77 against 41.30, 2.8 standard errors); the mean of the estimated variance is 0.2857 where the article reports 0.2819 (6.5 standard errors); the smallest attainable variance for this design is 0.2869. The article’s sequence, step for step, is no closer: its mean final sample sizes are -3.1, 1.5, and 4.1 standard errors from the table’s, and its mean estimated variance is 0.2856 (6.7). The differences are small, at most 1.3 percent for the first passage option and 1.6 percent for the article’s sequence, but the largest are outside Monte Carlo error under both, so the package’s reading of the sequence is not what separates it from the table. What does could not be determined from the article. The cost that the table implies is reproduced by the article’s sequence, which spent 4,976.5 of the 5,000 on average against the implied 4,976.9 (-1.3 standard errors). The first passage option spent 4,975.5 (-3.4), and the default 4,989.0.

What the article claims for the procedure does hold: no study exceeded the budget (100 percent within it under the first passage rule and 100 under the default), and the coverage of the 95% interval was 0.948 and 0.948. The default is the package’s choice and not the article’s procedure; the help page of seq_budget() gives the reasons.

The Gini Index: Chattopadhyay and De (2016)

The interval for the Gini index is the procedure of Chattopadhyay and De (2016). Their simulation study draws from three populations: a gamma distribution with shape 2.649 and rate 0.84, a lognormal distribution with log mean 2.185 and log standard deviation 0.562, and a Pareto distribution with scale 20,000 and shape 5. For each, the study computed the Gini index and the asymptotic variance of its estimator (the article’s Equation 6) by numerical integration, with no package code. The table compares those population values with the mean of gini_index() and the mean of the variance estimate that seq_aipe_gini() reports, over 2,000 samples of 2,000 observations.

The article’s interval is the estimate plus and minus the half width, 0.01. seq_aipe_gini() reports a different interval, the estimate plus and minus z times its estimated standard error, as the package’s other procedures do. When the rule is met that interval is never wider than the target, and the smaller the sample in which the rule is met, the narrower it is. The table therefore counts coverage twice in the same studies: for the article’s interval (the gini row plus and minus 0.01), which is what compares with the posted table, and for the interval the package reports.

Final sample size. The lognormal and Pareto rows are reproduced (0.4 and -0.7 standard errors). The gamma row is not. The package’s mean final sample size is 1,282.7 against 1,259.5, 1.8 percent higher and 4.9 standard errors away, and its standard deviation is 83 where the posted standard error implies 195 (for the lognormal population the two are 180 and 185, and for the Pareto population 206 and 189). The largest final sample sizes are similar (1,634 here and 1,594 in the posted version), which suggests that the posted gamma studies include final sample sizes well below the smallest found here (1,064). The cause cannot be settled without the code behind the posted table.

Coverage. The article’s interval covers 0.8870, 0.9065, and 0.8810 of the time for the gamma, lognormal, and Pareto populations against the posted 0.878, 0.9015, and 0.9018 (0.9, 0.5, and -2.2 standard errors). The interval the package reports covers 0.8830, 0.9025, and 0.8605. For the gamma and lognormal populations the two intervals hardly differ: the package’s has a mean width of 0.0198 and 0.0199 where the article’s is 0.02. For the Pareto population, where the rule is met in smaller samples (650 observations on average), its mean width is 0.0191, and it covers 2.0 percentage points less often than the article’s interval in the same studies. The coverage of the procedure at wide targets is in the last section.

Two Stage Procedures With Exact Properties

Four of the two stage procedures from Mukhopadhyay and de Silva (2009) have properties that hold exactly, not only in large samples: Stein’s (1945) interval for a normal mean (ts_fwd_norm_mean()), the interval for the location of a negative exponential distribution (ts_fwd_nexp_mean()), and the bounded risk procedures for a normal mean (ts_br_norm_mean()) and an exponential mean (ts_br_exp_mean(); the book’s Section 8.3.2, Equation 8.3.13). In each the total sample size depends on the first stage through one statistic whose distribution is known, so the expected sample size and the coverage or the risk can be computed exactly. The study does that calculation in base R, with no package code, and compares it with what the package’s functions did in simulated studies: a first stage, the total sample size the function asks for, a second stage of that size, and the final interval or estimate.

Of the 20 simulated values of the first runs, 19 are within two standard errors of the exact ones and 19 within three. Under the rule described at the top of the page, a condition with a value more than three standard errors from its exact value was run a second time. That happened once: the coverage of ts_fwd_norm_mean() (half width 0.2, 95%, first stage of 30) was 0.9478 in the first 100,000 studies, 3.4 standard errors below the exact 0.9502, and 0.9502 in the second 1,000,000 (z = 0.4). The second run agrees with the exact value, so the first difference was chance. The exact values themselves show the guarantees: coverage is at least 0.95 in every interval row (from 0.9502 to 0.9578), and the risk is at most the bound in every bounded risk row (from 0.940 to 0.993 of it). The row with n* = 44 and a first stage of 14 was chosen because it is where ts_br_exp_mean() comes closest to its bound: its help page reports an exact calculation over first stages of 3 to 100 and values of n* up to 2,000 in which the risk never exceeded the bound and was largest, 0.990 of it, for a first stage of 14 or 15 with n* near 44. The exact risk in that row is 0.9901 of the bound. For this procedure the bound rests on computation of that kind and not on a theorem, as the help page explains.

The other classical procedures (the purely sequential procedures for a mean, the purely sequential interval for a median, and the distribution free two stage interval) have asymptotic guarantees only. No published table is compared for them here; the last section measures them at wide targets.

Where the Package Departs From an Article

In several places the package does something other than what a source article prints. This section gives the evidence for four of them, each deliberate and documented in the help page of the function concerned. Three more are described elsewhere: the interval that seq_aipe_gini() reports, which is not the interval of its source article (the section on the Gini index above and the last section), the default allocation rule of the budget procedure (the section on the budget above and the help page of seq_budget()), and the power to which one factor is raised in the two cost sample sizes of the 2017 article (the help page of seq_mr_smd()).

A Variance Estimate That Is Zero or Negative

The estimate of the asymptotic variance on which a stopping rule rests can be zero or negative in a small sample. The articles replace it with a small positive number, n-3, and evaluate the rule, under which a study can stop at once with an interval far narrower than its data support. The package reports such a check as not met, so sampling continues (a positive estimate, however small, is used as the articles prescribe). The study followed the same 10,000 simulated studies under both rules for the Pearson correlation at ρ = 0.5 and a width of 0.2, taking the rule as printed from the flag that seq_aipe_r() sets when the variance estimate is unusable.

Rule Replications N, article N, simulated (SE) z Coverage, article Coverage, simulated (SE) z Width, article Width, simulated z
Rule as printed 10,000 204.0 205.2 (0.5) 1.3 0.9012 0.9021 (0.0030) 0.2 0.1938 0.1940 0.4
Package 10,000 204.0 206.7 (0.5) 3.0 0.9012 0.9089 (0.0029) 1.5 0.1938 0.1961 5.5

Under the rule as printed, 1.73 percent of the studies stopped on an unusable variance estimate. With those stops the rule as printed gives the article’s row (mean final sample size at 1.3 standard errors, coverage at 0.2, mean width at 0.4); without them the package’s studies are a little longer, cover a little more often (0.909 against 0.902), and end with intervals that are wider on average (0.1961 against 0.1940), because the intervals of the early stops were far narrower than the target.

The Variance of the Coefficient of Variation

Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2016, Equation 9, p. 631) and Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018, Equation 30, p. 233) give different expressions for the asymptotic variance of the sample coefficient of variation. The 2018 expression minus the 2016 one is (kurtosis − 3) κ2 (1 − κ2) / 4, where κ is the coefficient of variation: the two agree when the kurtosis of the population is 3, as it is for a normal population (and when κ is exactly 1), and differ otherwise. For a gamma population with a coefficient of variation of 0.8 the two expressions give 0.3036 and 0.5248. Simulation settles which describes the estimator: n times its mean squared error in samples of 2,000 was 0.5242 (standard error 0.0024).

The default of seq_mr_cv() therefore estimates the 2018 expression, and variance = "published" estimates the 2016 one, as the last two rows of the table confirm. “Optimal n” is the sample size that minimizes the risk when the population is known: the article computes it from its Equation 9 and the package from Equation 30, rounded up. For the normal populations the two agree and so do the two procedures, within 1.2 percent in mean final sample size. For the gamma and lognormal populations the article’s optimal sample size is too small, and its procedure stops early: at a coefficient of variation of 0.8 the published variance stops at a mean of 373 observations and the default at 478, where the risk is smallest near 513. Risk efficiency is the realized risk divided by the smallest attainable risk (standard errors of about 0.007). The risk is flat near its minimum, so stopping early costs less than the sample sizes suggest: with the published variance the risk efficiency is 1.02 to 1.04 for the gamma populations and 1.14 for the lognormal one, against 1.00 to 1.01 with the default. The option exists so that the article’s results, and those of DMAR::mr_cv(), which implements the article’s rule, can be reproduced.

Equation 26 of the 2018 Article

Equation 26 of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018, p. 232), the asymptotic variance of the standardized mean difference, omits a factor of one half in its second term. The authors’ correction is posted at https://kenkelley.org/wp-content/uploads/articles/Kelley_Darku_Chattopadhyay_Equation_26.pdf and ships with the package (system.file("eq26_correction.pdf", package = "SMSD")). The two forms differ only when the groups differ in mean and in skewness. For two populations with unit variance, a standardized mean difference of 0.5, and skewness in opposite directions (a standardized chi square with 3 degrees of freedom and its mirror image), the corrected form gives 1.3710 and the printed form 0.5545.

The Stopping Rule for the Squared Multiple Correlation

For the Wald interval the article’s Equation 63 (p. 505), as printed, stops at the first n that is at least (16 z2 / w2) (R2 + 1/n) (1 − (R2 + 1/n))2, where w is the target width and z the normal quantile for the confidence level. seq_aipe_R2() uses (R2 + 1/n) (1 − R2 + 1/n)2 in its place: the correction 1/n is added inside the second factor, where the printed form subtracts it. The two forms differ most when the population value is large. The study evaluated the printed form on the estimates that seq_aipe_R2() reports at each stage, for the two rows with 2 predictors and a population value of 0.9:

Equation 63 as printed Replications N, article N, simulated (SE) z Coverage, article Coverage, simulated (SE) z Width, article Width, simulated z
Table 13, 90% 5,000 68.66 66.34 (0.03) -22.8 0.8678 0.8766 (0.0047) 1.3 0.0733 0.0759 7.9
Table 14, 95% 5,000 84.17 79.91 (0.06) -26.4 0.9222 0.9366 (0.0034) 2.8 0.0790 0.0823 10.9

The printed form gives mean final sample sizes of 66.34 and 79.91, which are 23 and 26 standard errors below the article’s 68.66 and 84.17 and barely above the pilot sample sizes of 66 and 79. The form the package uses gives 68.58 and 84.04 for the same rows (-0.7 and -0.8 standard errors from the article), and reproduces the other Wald rows shown earlier. The package therefore implements the form that the article’s tables were evidently computed with, and its help page says so.

What the Procedures Do Not Guarantee at Wide Targets

The sequential intervals for effect sizes deliver the requested width by construction: the final interval is never wider than the target. Their coverage is a different kind of property. The articles prove that it approaches the confidence level as the target width shrinks, that is, as the sample the rule asks for grows. They do not prove, and it is not true, that coverage is close to the confidence level at every width. When the rule is met in a small sample, coverage can be far below nominal.

The table gives the coverage of 95% intervals measured in this study, with the default pilot sample size unless the row says otherwise, and the mean final sample size (per group for the standardized mean difference and the contrast, pairs for the correlations and the slope). “Skewed” data are standardized chi square variables with 3 degrees of freedom. The help pages of the functions report separate runs of some of these designs, often rounded to two decimals. A figure there can differ from the one here by up to about 0.02, several times the standard errors shown here, because each run has its own Monte Carlo error and some of those runs are smaller than these.

What the table shows, stated plainly:

  • Where the shortfall is small. For the standardized mean difference, the standardized mean, and the contrast, coverage is between 0.935 and 0.950 in the 4 conditions above. The lowest is the contrast at a width of 1, which stops with about 23 observations per group.
  • The Pearson correlation. At a correlation of 0.4 coverage is 0.78 at a width of 0.4 and 0.93 at 0.2. A stronger correlation is estimated with less sampling error, so the rule is met sooner and coverage is worse at the same width: 0.69 and 0.69 at 0.8, and 0.43 at a correlation of 0.9 with a width of 0.1. Skewed data lower it further (0.71 at 0.4 and a width of 0.4).
  • The regression slope behaves like the correlation: 0.83 for a slope of 0.5 at a width of 0.4, 0.71 with skewed data, and 0.61 for a slope of 2 at a width of 0.2.
  • The rank correlations fall short at a strong association too: 0.91 (Kendall) and 0.85 (Spearman) at ρ = 0.8 and a width of 0.4.
  • The coefficient of variation is sensitive to skewness. At a value of 0.5 coverage is 0.88 for gamma data and 0.79 for lognormal data at a width of 0.2, and still 0.86 for lognormal data at 0.1, with a mean of 322 observations.
  • The Gini index covers 0.90 and 0.92 of the time at widths of 0.2 and 0.1. That is the interval seq_aipe_gini() reports, which is not the interval of Chattopadhyay and De (2016); the two are set side by side below.
  • The squared multiple correlation fails badly when the number of predictors is not small beside the sample size the width calls for: for a population value of 0.5 at a width of 0.3 coverage is 0.85 with 5 predictors, 0.66 with 10, and 0.35 with 15, and at a width of 0.2 it is 0.87 with 10. The procedure also assumes multivariate normal data.
  • The distribution free two stage interval for a mean (ts_fwd_dfr_mean()) plugs the first stage variance into the known variance sample size with no allowance for having estimated it. With a first stage of 30 its coverage for a narrow target is 0.940 for normal data (the exact value is 0.941), 0.911 for exponential data, and 0.877 for lognormal data with a skewness of 4. Narrowing the target does not remove the shortfall while the first stage stays at 30; a larger first stage reduces it.

The Gini Index: Two Intervals

The interval of Chattopadhyay and De (2016) is the estimate plus and minus half the target width. seq_aipe_gini() reports the estimate plus and minus z times its estimated standard error, which the stopping rule keeps below the target, and well below it when the rule is met in a small sample. The study ran the two wide conditions above again through seq_aipe_gini_pilot() and seq_aipe_gini(), with new data, and counted the coverage of both intervals in the same studies.

Condition Quantity Mean N Coverage (SE) Replications Note
lognormal; width 0.2 coverage of the interval the package reports 30.4 0.890 (0.003) 10,000 mean width 0.1405
lognormal; width 0.2 coverage of the article’s interval 30.4 0.986 (0.001) 10,000
lognormal; width 0.1 coverage of the interval the package reports 88.0 0.916 (0.003) 10,000 mean width 0.0866
lognormal; width 0.1 coverage of the article’s interval 88.0 0.960 (0.002) 10,000

At a target width of 0.2 the interval the package reports has a mean width of 0.1405 and covers 0.890 of the time; the article’s interval covers 0.986 in the same studies. At 0.1 the two figures are 0.916 (mean width 0.0866) and 0.960. At these targets the shortfall belongs to the interval the package reports and not to the article’s procedure, whose interval covers more often than its nominal level here. The article’s interval can be formed from the package’s output: it is the gini row plus and minus half of width, once the rule is met.

The Purely Sequential Classical Procedures

The purely sequential procedures from Mukhopadhyay and de Silva (2009) check their rule after every observation. Their confidence level, their risk bound, or their optimality holds in the limit as the target narrows, and none of them has a *_sensitivity() function, so the study ran each through its pilot function and its check function, with the default pilot, at a target near the least favorable one that its help page reports. In the table n* is the sample size that would be needed if the population were known. For an interval the target is the nominal 0.95. For the bounded risk procedure it is a risk of at most 1 times the bound, and for the minimum risk procedures it is a risk close to 1 times the smallest attainable.

Procedure and condition Quantity Mean N Value (SE) Replications
seq_fwd_norm_mean() normal, standard deviation 2; half width 0.77 (n* = 26) coverage 24.2 0.923 (0.001) 40,000
seq_fwd_norm_mean() normal, standard deviation 2; half width 0.25 (n* = 246) coverage 245.0 0.948 (0.002) 10,000
seq_fwd_dfr_mean() normal, standard deviation 2; half width 0.5 (n* = 61) coverage 59.9 0.939 (0.002) 20,000
seq_fwd_dfr_mean() exponential, standard deviation 2; half width 0.5 (n* = 61) coverage 52.4 0.854 (0.002) 20,000
seq_fwd_dfr_mean() exponential, standard deviation 2; half width 0.25 (n* = 246) coverage 238.8 0.934 (0.002) 10,000
seq_fwd_nexp_mean() negative exponential, scale 2; width 0.24 (n* = 25) coverage 24.4 0.932 (0.001) 40,000
seq_blci_dfr_median() standard normal; d = 0.2456 (n* = 100) coverage 97.5 0.924 (0.003) 10,000
seq_blci_dfr_median() unit exponential; d = 0.196 (n* = 100) coverage 95.6 0.917 (0.003) 10,000
seq_blci_dfr_median() standard normal; d = 0.08685 (n* = 800) coverage 761.8 0.932 (0.004) 5,000
seq_br_norm_mean() normal, standard deviation 3; squared error loss, A = 2, w = 0.65 (n* = 28) risk relative to the bound 25.8 1.217 (0.009) 50,000
seq_br_norm_mean() normal, standard deviation 3; absolute error loss, A = 2, w = 0.92 (n* = 27) risk relative to the bound 25.2 1.086 (0.004) 50,000
seq_mr_norm_mean() normal, standard deviation 1; A = 100, c = 1 (n* = 10) risk relative to the smallest attainable 9.4 1.070 (0.004) 50,000
seq_mr_exp_mean() exponential, mean 1; A = 225, c = 1 (n* = 15) risk relative to the smallest attainable 14.5 1.150 (0.004) 50,000
  • The fixed width interval for a normal mean (seq_fwd_norm_mean()) covers 0.923 of the time when about 26 observations are needed and 0.948 when about 246 are. Stein’s two stage interval, ts_fwd_norm_mean(), is the alternative whose level is guaranteed.
  • The distribution free interval for a mean (seq_fwd_dfr_mean()) covers 0.939 for normal data when about 61 observations are needed. For exponential data with the same standard deviation it covers 0.854 at that target and 0.934 when about 246 are needed: skewness slows the approach to the stated level considerably.
  • The interval for the location of a negative exponential distribution (seq_fwd_nexp_mean()) covers 0.932 when about 25 observations are needed. Here too the two stage interval, ts_fwd_nexp_mean(), has a guaranteed level.
  • The interval for a median (seq_blci_dfr_median()) has at least its stated coverage at any fixed sample size, but the sequential procedure stops when the interval happens to be short. Its coverage is 0.917 to 0.932 in the three conditions above, and the shortfall does not go away quickly: it is 0.932 in the condition that ends with about 762 observations.
  • The bounded risk procedure for a normal mean (seq_br_norm_mean()) approaches its bound from above. When the bound calls for about 28 observations under squared error loss the risk is 1.22 times the bound, and when it calls for about 27 under absolute error loss it is 1.09 times the bound. The two stage procedure ts_br_norm_mean() keeps its risk at or below the bound for normal data, as the exact results above show.
  • The minimum risk procedures attain the smallest risk only in the limit: the risk of seq_mr_norm_mean() is 1.07 times the smallest attainable when the best sample size is 10, and that of seq_mr_exp_mean() is 1.15 times when it is
    1. (seq_mr_nexp_mean() and seq_mr_dfr_mean_arb() are not in the study; their help pages report the same kind of figures.)

What Helps

A larger pilot sample helps where the shortfall comes from stopping early. A minimum pilot sample size of 40 raised coverage from 0.78 to 0.90 for the correlation of 0.4 at a width of 0.4, and from 0.83 to 0.92 for the slope of 0.5, at a cost of 8 and 9 more pairs on average. It is not a cure for a strong relationship or for skewed data.

The practical rule follows from the tables. Before relying on an interval at a planned width, run the matching *_sensitivity() function at each true value that is plausible for the study, the strongest included, with data as skewed as the study’s are likely to be, and read its coverage row. If coverage is low, plan a narrower width, a larger minimum pilot sample size, or both. For a classical procedure, which has no such function, the help page gives its measured coverage or risk over a range of targets, and where a two stage procedure with an exact guarantee exists it is named there.

Reproducing This Article

The study is one script. From the root of the package’s repository, with the package’s source loaded or the package installed:

Rscript -e 'devtools::load_all(quiet = TRUE); source("data-raw/validation_study.R")'

It writes data-raw/validation_results.rds, a data frame with one row per comparison (the procedure, the source with its table and page, the condition, the published value and its standard error, the package’s value and its standard error, the number of replications, and z), with the seed, the date, and the package version as attributes. The replication counts are in the tables above; the cached file was made on 2026-10-10 with SMSD 1.0.0 under R version 4.6.1 (2026-06-24). Every part of every condition sets its own seed, so a second run of the script gives the same numbers. The script uses 6 cores unless the environment variable SMSD_VALIDATION_CORES says otherwise. On Windows, where R cannot run the parts as forked processes, it uses one core and takes several hours. The script’s header describes settings for a shorter trial run or for some conditions only; this article refuses a cache made that way.
